Name: latent_reasoning_pivot
Title: The Latent Pivot: Do Multilingual LLMs Reason in a Language-Agnostic Space or a Dominant-Language Scaffold, and Can We Choose the Optimal One Per Problem?
Short Hypothesis: During chain-of-thought reasoning, multilingual LLMs pass through intermediate-layer states whose 'latent reasoning language' (the language a logit-lens/PatchScopes decode reveals) is not fixed but problem-dependent, and the correctness of a given problem depends causally on which latent pivot language the model transits. We hypothesize we can (1) read out a per-token 'latent language' trajectory during reasoning, (2) show correctness correlates with transiting through a specific pivot language (often English/high-resource) that varies by problem type and prompt language, and (3) causally steer the latent reasoning language mid-generation to improve accuracy on the language and problems where the model's default pivot is suboptimal.
Related Work: Wang et al. (2025) study surface-level language mixing in reasoning traces and show forcing Latin/Han scripts via constrained decoding helps, and that output script aligns with internal representations. Hakimov et al. (2025) note open-weight models switch to English for internal reasoning. He et al. (2026) use SAEs to steer a reasoning latent (monolingual). Existing multilingual-reasoning transfer methods (SoT) convert queries into language-agnostic structures at the prompt level. What is missing: a token-level, layerwise causal characterization of the *internal* reasoning language (not the emitted tokens) using logit-lens/PatchScopes, a demonstration that the latent pivot is problem- and prompt-language-dependent (not globally English), and a training-free intervention that steers the latent pivot mid-reasoning rather than constraining decoding of surface tokens. This shifts the analysis from observable output script to the hidden computational scaffold and makes it causal and per-problem-optimizable.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs solve reasoning tasks regardless of the prompt language, but it remains unclear whether the underlying computation is genuinely language-agnostic or scaffolded on a dominant language. Prior work has documented surface-level 'language mixing' in reasoning traces and shown that forcing a particular output script can help. We go beneath the surface: using logit-lens and PatchScopes decodes of intermediate-layer states, we extract a token-level, layerwise trajectory of the *latent reasoning language*—the language the model is internally 'thinking in' at each reasoning step, independent of the tokens it emits. Across four open multilingual models and reasoning benchmarks translated into ten languages spanning scripts and resource levels, we test three claims: (1) the latent pivot language is not globally fixed but varies with problem type and prompt language; (2) per-problem correctness is predictable from the latent trajectory, with a beneficial pivot that differs across problem categories; and (3) we can causally steer the latent reasoning language mid-generation via activation addition of language-direction vectors, improving accuracy on prompt languages and problem types whose default pivot is suboptimal, without constraining the surface output. We contrast internal-state steering against surface script constraining to show they are distinct mechanisms. Deliverables: a latent-language read-out method, a mapping of which pivots help which problems in which languages, and a training-free intervention yielding accuracy gains, especially for low-resource prompt languages. This reframes multilingual reasoning as controllable at the level of an internal linguistic scaffold.
Experiments: 1) Latent-language read-out: For open multilingual models (Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B), during greedy CoT generation on each problem, at every reasoning-token position apply logit-lens and PatchScopes to intermediate layers and classify the decoded top-k vocabulary distribution by language (using a fastText/langid classifier over decoded token strings), producing a per-token x per-layer latent-language trajectory. Validate the read-out on control prompts where the intended internal language is known (e.g., translation tasks). 2) Datasets: MGSM (math) and a multilingual commonsense/logic set (e.g., translated StrategyQA and XCOPA-style items) rendered in 10 languages (English, German, Spanish, Russian, Hindi, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Swahili, Turkish). 3) Descriptive analysis: quantify the dominant latent pivot per (model, prompt language, problem type); test whether pivot is fixed vs. variable using entropy of pivot distribution and chi-square by problem category. 4) Predictive analysis: train a simple logistic classifier from latent-trajectory features (fraction of tokens in each latent language per layer band) to predict per-problem correctness; report AUC and identify which pivots are associated with higher accuracy for each problem type/prompt language (beneficial-pivot map). 5) Causal steering: compute per-language 'language direction' vectors as difference-of-means of residual-stream activations between parallel same-content generations in different languages; during reasoning add the direction of a target pivot (e.g., English or the language the beneficial-pivot map recommends) at mid layers for the first N reasoning tokens; measure accuracy change per prompt language and problem type. 6) Mechanism contrast: compare latent steering (hidden-state) against surface script/language constraining a la Wang et al. (constrained decoding to a target language) on identical items to show they produce different accuracy and different latent trajectories; also compare against no-intervention baseline. 7) Ablations: layer choice, number of steered tokens, steering strength; verify steering changes the read-out latent language as intended (manipulation check). Metrics: reasoning accuracy (exact-match/answer accuracy), correctness-prediction AUC from latent features, pivot entropy, and per-language accuracy delta from steering.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Logit-lens/PatchScopes decodes are noisy proxies for 'internal language'; mitigated by validation on known-language control tasks and by using PatchScopes which decodes into natural language more faithfully. 2) Language classification of decoded tokens can be unreliable for short/subword tokens; mitigate with top-k aggregation, character n-gram langid, and reporting confidence-thresholded results. 3) The latent pivot may simply always be English for these models, weakening the 'problem-dependent' claim; even a null result (English-scaffold universality) is a publishable, clarifying finding, and we design analyses to detect either outcome. 4) Steering may degrade fluency or produce off-target effects; we include manipulation checks and fluency/answer-format filters. 5) Difference-of-means language directions may entangle content with language; we control content by using parallel translations of identical problems. 6) Effects may be model-specific; we report across four models to assess generality.
